items.title: Anatomical defect and clinical relevance
items.contentHtml:
Umbilical aponeurotic ring

The umbilical aponeurotic ring is a defect in the linea alba at the level of the navel, through which peritoneal content protrudes. In adults, weakness is associated with increased intra-abdominal pressure (obesity, ascites, pregnancy, exertion). The hernial sac usually contains omentum or small intestine; The neck of the defect is rigid and fibrous, which predisposes it to incarceration. On examination, the defect is palpated as a hole in the umbilical ring, prompting the Valsalva maneuver. Defect diameter >2 cm increases the risk of complications. Elective surgical repair is indicated to avoid incarceration, especially in adults with symptoms or progressive defect.

items.title: Typical hernia content
items.contentHtml:
Contents of the hernial sac

The most common content is the omentum (greater omentum) or the small intestine (jejunum-ileum loops). The incarcerated omentum produces a firm, non-reducible mass, with dull pain, but without intestinal obstruction. The incarcerated small intestine may progress to mechanical obstruction, with cramping pain, vomiting, and distention. In adult umbilical hernia, the contents are usually omentum, but the small intestine is associated with a greater risk of strangulation. On ultrasound, peristalsis is identified in the contents if it is intestine; the absence of peristalsis suggests ischemia. Computed tomography (CT) differentiates omentum (fat density) from intestinal loop (enhancing wall).

items.title: Incarceration: definition and approach
items.contentHtml:
Hernia incarceration

Incarceration is a non-reducible hernia, with contents trapped in the sac, but without immediate vascular compromise. It manifests as an irreducible painful umbilical mass. The pain is constant or cramping if there is obstruction. Manual reduction is contraindicated if there are signs of strangulation (fever, tachycardia, peritonism). In the absence of alarm data, gentle reduction with sedation can be attempted, but recurrence is high. Elective repair is indicated after successful reduction. In incarcerated umbilical hernia in adults, the risk of progression to strangulation is greater than in children, so early surgery is the rule.

items.title: Strangulation: pathophysiological sequence
items.contentHtml:
Hernial strangulation

Strangulation implies vascular compromise of the hernial contents, leading to ischemia, necrosis and eventual perforation. The mechanism is compression of the neck of the sac on the mesenteric vessels, first venous and then arterial. Clinically, the pain becomes intense and continuous, with signs of peritoneal irritation. Intestinal necrosis releases toxins and bacteria, which can cause sepsis. Perforation produces peritonitis and local abscess. In strangulated umbilical hernia, mortality is high if it is not operated immediately. The presence of peritoneal signs indicates a surgical emergency. The tomography shows lack of enhancement of the intestinal wall and pneumoperitoneum if there is perforation.

items.title: Clinical picture of obstruction
items.contentHtml:
Acute abdominal pain and obstruction

Incarcerated umbilical hernia may present as acute abdominal pain with distal intestinal obstruction. Symptoms include periumbilical cramping pain, vomiting (initially gastric, then bilious), abdominal distension, and absence of bowel movements or gas. On auscultation, there are fighting (metallic) intestinal sounds in the initial phases, which disappear in late paralytic ileus. Palpation reveals a painful, irreducible umbilical mass. It is crucial to examine all hernias in every patient with intestinal obstruction. The abdominal x-ray shows dilated loops with air-fluid levels. The tomography confirms the transition site and the presence of complications.

items.title: Clinical diagnosis of umbilical mass
items.contentHtml:
Irreducible painful umbilical mass

The classic triad is irreducible painful umbilical mass with signs of obstruction. On examination, the mass is firm, tense, with erythematous skin if inflammation is present. The differential diagnosis includes: umbilical lipoma, urachus cyst, Sister Mary Joseph metastasis (gastric or ovarian carcinoma), and hematoma. Irreducibility alone does not equate to strangulation, but with pain and systemic signs (fever, tachycardia) it suggests compromise. Abdominal wall ultrasound is useful to confirm the defect and contents. Tomography is the gold standard for evaluating complications. When in doubt, surgical exploration is indicated.

items.title: Peritonism: surgical emergency
items.contentHtml:
Peritoneal signs

The presence of peritoneal signs (pain on decompression, abdominal rigidity, absence of sounds) indicates peritonitis, which in the context of an umbilical hernia points to strangulation with necrosis or perforation. These signs are an emergency and require urgent laparotomy or laparoscopy, without delay for imaging studies if the patient is unstable. Surgical delay increases morbidity and mortality. Intraoperatively, intestinal viability is evaluated; If there is necrosis, resection with anastomosis is performed. Repair of the defect is done with mesh if there is no contamination; in case of peritonitis, primary or delayed repair is preferred.

items.title: Abdominal x-ray in obstruction
items.contentHtml:
Simple abdominal radiography

In intestinal obstruction due to umbilical hernia, radiography of the abdomen in recumbency and standing shows dilated loops (>3 cm in diameter in the small intestine) with fluid-air levels in a staircase. The distribution of dilated loops depends on the level of obstruction; In umbilical hernia, they are usually central or in the upper abdomen. The absence of gas in the distal colon suggests complete obstruction. However, radiography has low sensitivity in identifying the hernia as the cause. Computed tomography (CT) is more accurate. X-ray is useful as a first evaluation, but should not delay surgery if there are warning signs.

items.title: Computed Tomography (CT)
items.contentHtml:
Computed tomography

Abdominal computed tomography (CT) with intravenous contrast is the study of choice to confirm the diagnosis and evaluate complications. Key findings: defect in the abdominal wall at the umbilical level, hernial sac with contents (omentum or intestinal loop), and signs of strangulation such as thickening of the intestinal wall, lack of mural enhancement, gas in the wall (intestinal pneumatosis) or free fluid. CT also detects pneumoperitoneum if perforation is present. In patients with obesity or clinical doubt, CT is decisive. Sensitivity is high to differentiate incarcerated hernia from other causes of umbilical mass. With oral contrast (optional) the obstruction can be assessed.

items.title: Risk in adults vs children
items.contentHtml:
Umbilical hernia in adults

The umbilical hernia in adults has a greater risk of incarceration and strangulation than that in children. While in children the majority close spontaneously before the age of 4-5, in adults the defect does not resolve and tends to increase. Risk factors: obesity, ascites, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), constipation, and multiparity. Incarceration occurs in 10-20% of adults, and strangulation in 30% of incarcerated individuals. Therefore, elective repair is recommended in all symptomatic adults, and in asymptomatic adults if the defect is large (>2 cm) or there are comorbidities. Urgent surgery is reserved for complications.

items.title: Indications for urgent surgery
items.contentHtml:
Urgent surgery

Urgent surgery is indicated if strangulation is suspected (severe pain, peritoneal signs, signs of complete obstruction, fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis, acidosis). The procedure consists of herniotomy, inspection of the contents, and intestinal resection if necrosis is present. Viability is evaluated by color, peristalsis and bleeding on cut; If in doubt, warm saline can be applied and reassessed. In case of frank peritonitis, midline laparotomy is performed to explore the entire intestine. Repair of the defect with mesh is contraindicated in contaminated fields; Primary suture or two-stage repair is preferred.

items.title: Elective repair with mesh
items.contentHtml:
Elective repair

In reducible or asymptomatic umbilical hernias, mesh repair is the gold standard in adults, with a lower recurrence rate than primary suture (Mayo technique). The repair can be open or laparoscopic; Laparoscopic surgery offers less postoperative pain and hospital stay. Polypropylene or composite mesh is used, placed in a preperitoneal or intraperitoneal position (if laparoscopic). Preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis (cefazolin 2 g IV) is administered within 60 minutes before the incision. In patients with obesity, preoperative weight loss improves outcomes. Elective surgery avoids urgency and its complications.
